analysis.one_liner: Bars drugmakers from restricting access to their drugs for companies developing cheaper generics and biosimilars.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never advanced before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Some brand-name drugmakers use safety programs and distribution rules to refuse selling small samples of their drugs to companies trying to develop generic or biosimilar copies. That delays competition and keeps prices high after patents expire. This bill would require drugmakers to sell testers the quantities they request at normal market prices, help create shared safety programs for generics, and let blocked developers sue for triple damages. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who would see generic and biosimilar competition arrive sooner, which typically means lower prices at the pharmacy. Also generic and biosimilar manufacturers, who would gain guaranteed access to the brand-name products they need to run required testing, and the FDA, which would gain a clearer structure for authorizing testing of drugs with safety restrictions.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it a condition of FDA approval that a drug's license holder not apply distribution restrictions in any way that cuts off supply of the drug to a developer seeking to test a generic, biosimilar, or follow-on product.

For drugs whose safety programs limit distribution, license holders must fill testing requests within 30 days at a nondiscriminatory, commercially reasonable, market-based price, or the FDA can issue the tester an individual authorization to obtain the product.

The bill requires brand-name and generic companies to negotiate in good faith toward a single, shared safety program (a shared REMS) rather than letting the brand company stall a generic's entry, and it gives an aggrieved developer the right to sue for injunctive relief and treble damages.
The bill's findings state that these access restrictions deter and delay development of affordable drugs and extend patent-based monopolies beyond their lawful patent life.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drugmakers, whose ability to use safety programs and distribution restrictions to slow generic and biosimilar competition would be curtailed, with enforcement through lawsuits carrying treble damages. Consumers see no direct cost under the bill; the cost to brand makers would come through faster competition and lower prices.

drawbacks.text: Safety programs with distribution restrictions exist for genuinely risky drugs, and critics of forced-access rules argue that pushing samples out through ordinary wholesalers could weaken safeguards for dangerous medicines. The bill answers this by requiring FDA review for testing that involves human trials, letting the Secretary block a transfer that presents an imminent public-health hazard, and shielding license holders from liability for testers' safety failures.

The treble-damages enforcement mechanism could invite litigation over what counts as a 'commercially reasonable' price or 'good faith' negotiation, imposing legal costs on drugmakers even where the underlying safety concerns were legitimate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is faster generic and biosimilar competition, which is one of the most reliable ways to lower drug prices, and the bill is built to preserve safety: testing that involves human trials needs FDA authorization, the FDA can stop any transfer that is an imminent hazard, and the brand maker is not liable for testers' safety failures. The serious cost falls on brand-name drugmakers' profits, which is the point. The main design risk is litigation over vague terms like 'commercially reasonable,' not patient safety.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote, so the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative Peter Welch introduced the FAST Generics Act on February 5, 2019, joined by Representatives David McKinley and David Cicilline, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
The bill attracted 4 cosponsors in total: 3 Democrats and 1 Republican.
The action history shows no further activity after the committee referral — no subcommittee action, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 116th Congress.

The bill's findings state that license holders were restricting access to their products to delay generic and biosimilar development and extend monopolies beyond the lawful patent term, and that existing FDA enforcement had been insufficient to stop these practices.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drugmakers kept the ability to use distribution restrictions and safety programs to delay generic and biosimilar competitors, and patients continued to pay brand-name prices for longer.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drugmakers and their patent extensions

for.name: Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: David McKinley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it Republican support.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Frank Pallone, D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral without any hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Democratic lead sponsor with a Republican and Democratic cosponsors — and its 4 cosponsors split 3 Democrats to 1 Republican; its demise came from inaction in committee, not a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill removes their ability to use distribution restrictions and safety programs to keep samples of their drugs away from generic and biosimilar developers, and exposes them to lawsuits with treble damages. Their gain from the status quo — a longer effective monopoly and higher prices — comes directly at the expense of patients and payers.

They would get guaranteed, prompt access to brand-name reference products at market-based prices, letting them complete required testing years sooner. Faster-to-market competitors benefit patients directly through lower prices.
